sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch. Correlation 'does not necessarily imply cause and effect'; a confounding variable can account for a relationship between two variables; a scientific experiment is 'the only way to establish that there is a cause-and-effect relationship', and random assignment lets differences between groups be attributed to the independent variable.

brief.situation: You help with the patient newsletter at Northshore Physical Therapy (fictional). Last quarter, patients could opt in to a reminder app. App users attended 92% of booked visits and non-users 71%. The draft says the app improves attendance, and the manager will buy it for every patient at 17:00. It is 16:05. All figures are invented teaching data.
handover: App users were younger on average and more often booked online.
The vendor offers a 3-month trial for half the patients.
howItWorks: Pick a step from the action list: look, change, check or ship. Nothing you pick is typed or executed: every step shows an authored result.
Each step takes working minutes, and the clock moves by the minutes it takes. The deadline runs on the same clock.
Shipping is final for this case. Afterwards you record what you found and explain your reasoning.

scoring.modelReasoning: Patients chose whether to use the app, so this is a correlational comparison. The groups differ in age and booking habits, and non-users attended about as poorly the year before, so confounders can explain the gap. Report an association, not a cause, and use the vendor's trial with random assignment before buying for everyone. Adjusting for age leaves other differences; the size of a gap does not make it causal.
